Do not turn missing information into a normal finding, a negative finding or a confirmed diagnosis. Distinguish hypotheses, proposed tests and conditional advice from claims about what was observed. Credit defensible alternatives; do not require exact reproduction of a reference. Apply only the requested criterion. Do not add unstated task requirements. If an ambiguous rubric interpretation affects the grade, state that interpretation explicitly. When THIS criterion has no original descriptor for a selected intermediate score, state that the choice is provisional; never invent an author-supplied descriptor. Do not claim descriptors are missing when they are present. Use Cannot assess when the available material does not support a defensible assessment; do not convert inability to assess into a low clinical score. Give only the final justification, not an internal deliberation trace.

Recorded clinician checkpoint BEFORE the patient reply (not patient-facing): 52-year-old man with 1-year history of watery diarrhoea (3–4/day), upper abdominal discomfort, distal numbness, and over 6 months progressive breathlessness, fatigue and 10 kg weight loss. Clinician: Could you tell me more about the numbness — is it in both feet, both hands, or both? Is it symmetric and has it been gradually worsening? Also, have you had an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) done, and if so, could I review that report?
Recorded clinician checkpoint BEFORE the patient reply (not patient-facing): 52-year-old man with chronic watery diarrhoea (1 year), distal numbness, progressive breathlessness, fatigue and 10 kg weight loss. Initial labs show elevated NT-proBNP (887 pg/mL) and mildly elevated hs-troponin T (23.9 ng/L), suggesting cardiac involvement, plus mild renal impairment (eGFR 62.7). The combination of chronic GI symptoms, peripheral neuropathy, cardiac dysfunction and weight loss raises concern for a systemic process such as AL amyloidosis, though other causes of malabsorption with secondary anaemia and cardiac strain remain possible. Echocardiography would help characterise the cardiac involvement. [certainty: uncertain]

Clinician: Have you had any blood tests looking for abnormal proteins — specifically serum free light chains, serum protein electrophoresis, or immunofixation? If so, could I review those results?
Recorded clinician checkpoint BEFORE the patient reply (not patient-facing): 52-year-old man with chronic watery diarrhoea, distal numbness, progressive breathlessness, fatigue, 10 kg weight loss, mild renal impairment, and echocardiography showing symmetric LV wall thickening (septum 14.1 mm), LVEF 36%, diastolic dysfunction, and relative apical sparing on strain. This constellation — multi-organ involvement (cardiac, GI, peripheral nerve, renal) with the characteristic apical-sparing strain pattern — is highly suggestive of systemic amyloidosis, most likely AL (light-chain) type. Confirmation requires demonstration of a monoclonal protein (serum/urine free light chains, immunofixation) and ideally tissue biopsy with Congo red staining. [certainty: working]

The differential now shifts toward hereditary ATTR (transthyretin) amyloidosis — which can present with neuropathy and cardiomyopathy — or AA amyloidosis secondary to a chronic inflammatory condition. Family history and history of chronic inflammation are key to distinguishing these. [certainty: working]
